\section{Introduction}

Carath\'eodory's theorem states that a point in the convex hull of a set
$S \subseteq \R^d$ already lies in the convex hull of at most $d+1$ points of
$S$. B\'ar\'any's \emph{Colorful Carath\'eodory Theorem} (1982) is a striking
refinement: given $d+1$ sets (``colors''), each containing a target point $x$ in
its convex hull, $x$ lies in the convex hull of a \emph{rainbow} selection --- one
point from each color. It is the engine behind Tverberg's theorem, the first
selection lemma, centerpoint results, and algorithmic questions in computational
geometry.

We focus on $x = 0$, the origin, which enjoys an extra symmetry: it is fixed by
scaling. This lets us pass freely between two notions of capturing the origin ---
\emph{convex} (nonnegative weights summing to one) and \emph{conical} (nonnegative
weights, not all zero). We prove these coincide for the origin (the
\emph{homogeneity bridge}, Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge}), prove the colorful theorem
for the origin in arbitrary finite dimension (Theorem~\ref{thm:main}), and deduce
the conical colorful theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:cone}), closing with explicit
statements in $\R^d$.

\section{Definitions and setting}

Throughout, $V$ is a real vector space; from Section~\ref{sec:core} onward it
carries an inner product $\ip{\cdot}{\cdot}$ with norm $\|v\| = \sqrt{\ip{v}{v}}$
and is finite-dimensional with $d := \dimop_\R V$. An index type $\iota$ (the
\emph{colors}) is finite of cardinality $r = |\iota|$; each color $i$ carries a
finite set $C_i \subseteq V$.

\begin{definition}[Conical capture of the origin]
A finite family $(p_i)_{i \in s}$ \emph{conically captures the origin}, written
$\ConicZero(s, p)$, if there are weights $w : s \to \R$ with $w_i \ge 0$ for all
$i \in s$, some $w_j > 0$, and $\sum_{i \in s} w_i\, p_i = 0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Convex capture of the origin]
The family \emph{convexly captures the origin}, written $\ConvexZero(s, p)$, if
there are weights $w : s \to \R$ with $w_i \ge 0$ for all $i \in s$,
$\sum_{i \in s} w_i = 1$, and $\sum_{i \in s} w_i\, p_i = 0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Colorful transversal]
Given color classes $(C_i)_{i \in \iota}$, a \emph{colorful transversal} is a map
$t : \iota \to V$ with $t_i \in C_i$ for every $i$. Its \emph{range} is
$\{t_i : i \in \iota\}$.
\end{definition}

\section{The homogeneity bridge}

\begin{theorem}[Homogeneity bridge]\label{thm:bridge}
For any finite family $(p_i)_{i \in s}$,
$\ConicZero(s, p) \iff \ConvexZero(s, p)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $w_i \ge 0$, not all zero, with $\sum_i w_i p_i = 0$. Let
$s^\star = \sum_{i \in s} w_i \ge w_j > 0$. Then $w'_i = w_i / s^\star$ satisfies
$w'_i \ge 0$, $\sum_i w'_i = 1$, and $\sum_i w'_i p_i = (1/s^\star)\sum_i w_i p_i
= 0$. ($\Leftarrow$) A convex combination has nonnegative weights summing to
$1 \ne 0$, so some $w_j > 0$, and the same vanishing combination witnesses
$\ConicZero(s, p)$.
\end{proof}

The result hinges on $\lambda \cdot 0 = 0$ for $\lambda > 0$: rescaling a
vanishing combination preserves vanishing. For a general target $x \ne 0$ the two
notions genuinely differ.

\section{From capture to convex hulls}

\begin{lemma}[Convex capture equals hull membership]\label{lem:hull}
For a finite set $s \subseteq V$,
$\ConvexZero(s, \mathrm{id}) \iff 0 \in \conv(s)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Unfolding the convex hull of a finite set as centers of mass of nonnegative weight
systems summing to one, both sides assert weights $w \ge 0$ with
$\sum_{x \in s} w_x = 1$ and $\sum_{x \in s} w_x\, x = 0$. The constraint
$\sum w_x = 1$ excludes the degenerate all-zero weighting.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Hull of a transversal's range]\label{lem:range}
Let $\iota$ be finite and $t : \iota \to V$. If
$0 \in \conv(\{t_i : i \in \iota\})$, then $\ConvexZero(\iota, t)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Hull membership provides a finitely supported weighting of points in the range.
Pulling back along $t$ (assigning to each color the weight of its image, $0$ off
the support) yields nonnegative color weights summing to one whose weighted sum of
the $t_i$ vanishes.
\end{proof}

\section{The colorful Carath\'eodory theorem for the origin}\label{sec:core}

We assume $V$ finite-dimensional, $d = \dimop_\R V$.

\begin{lemma}[Support on a hyperplane is small]\label{lem:small}
Let $p \ne 0$ and let $A \subseteq V$ be finite, affinely independent, with
$\ip{p}{a} = c$ for all $a \in A$ and a common constant $c$. Then $|A| \le d$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $f = \ip{p}{\cdot}$, a nonzero linear functional. It is onto (for any scalar
$\lambda$, $f((\lambda/\|p\|^2)p) = \lambda$), so $\rank f = 1$ and, by
rank--nullity, $\dimop \ker f = d - 1$. For $a, b \in A$, $f(a - b) = 0$, so all
differences lie in $\ker f$, whence $\vspan(A) \subseteq \ker f$ has dimension
$\le d - 1$. Affine independence gives $\dimop \vspan(A) + 1 = |A|$, so
$|A| \le d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Descent step]\label{lem:descent}
Let $K$ be convex, $p, y \in K$, $p \ne 0$, and $\ip{p}{y} < \|p\|^2$. Then there
is $q \in K$ with $\|q\| < \|p\|$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $q_\theta = (1-\theta)p + \theta y = p + \theta(y - p) \in K$ for
$\theta \in [0,1]$. Then
\[
\|q_\theta\|^2 = \|p\|^2 - 2\theta\big(\|p\|^2 - \ip{p}{y}\big) + \theta^2\|y - p\|^2.
\]
Let $\delta = \|p\|^2 - \ip{p}{y} > 0$ and $\varepsilon = \|y - p\|^2 > 0$. With
$\theta = \min(1, \delta/\varepsilon) > 0$ we have $\theta\varepsilon \le \delta$,
so $\|q_\theta\|^2 \le \|p\|^2 - \theta\delta < \|p\|^2$. Take $q = q_\theta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Supporting hyperplane at the projection]\label{lem:sep}
Let $K$ be convex and $p \in K$ realize the distance from the origin to $K$. Then
$\ip{p}{w} \ge \|p\|^2$ for all $w \in K$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The variational characterization of the nearest point gives
$\ip{0 - p}{w - p} \le 0$; expanding, $\ip{p}{w} \ge \|p\|^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Support finset on the supporting hyperplane]\label{lem:support}
Let $p \ne 0$, $s \subseteq V$, $p \in \conv(s)$, and $\|p\|^2 \le \ip{p}{x}$ for
all $x \in s$. Then there is finite $A \subseteq s$ with $p \in \conv(A)$ and
$|A| \le d$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By Carath\'eodory choose minimal affinely independent $A_0 \subseteq s$ with
$p = \sum_{a \in A_0} w_a a$, $w_a \ge 0$, $\sum_a w_a = 1$. Then
\[
0 = \ip{p}{p} - \|p\|^2 \sum_a w_a = \sum_{a \in A_0} w_a\big(\ip{p}{a} - \|p\|^2\big),
\]
a sum of nonnegative terms, so each vanishes: $w_a > 0 \Rightarrow \ip{p}{a} =
\|p\|^2$. Let $A = \{a \in A_0 : w_a \ne 0\}$; then $p \in \conv(A)$, $A$ is
affinely independent, and all its points lie on $\ip{p}{\cdot} = \|p\|^2$. Apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:small}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A color is free]\label{lem:pigeon}
Let $\iota$ be finite, $f : \iota \to V$, and $A \subseteq V$ finite with
$A \subseteq \{f_i\}$ and $|A| < |\iota|$. Then some color $j$ satisfies: every
$a \in A$ equals $f_i$ for some $i \ne j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose $\varphi(a)$ with $f_{\varphi(a)} = a$. If no color were free, $\varphi$
would be surjective onto $\iota$, forcing $|A| \ge |\iota|$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Near-side vertex]\label{lem:near}
If $0 \in \conv(C)$ for finite $C \subseteq V$ and $p \ne 0$, then some $y \in C$
has $\ip{p}{y} < \|p\|^2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Otherwise $C$ lies in the convex half-space $\{x : \ip{p}{x} \ge \|p\|^2\}$, which
then contains $\conv(C) \ni 0$; but $\ip{p}{0} = 0 < \|p\|^2$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Colorful Carath\'eodory for the origin]\label{thm:main}
Let $V$ be a $d$-dimensional real inner product space and $(C_i)_{i \in \iota}$
finite color classes with $|\iota| \ge d + 1$. If $0 \in \conv(C_i)$ for every
$i$, then there is a colorful transversal $t : \iota \to V$ with
$0 \in \conv(\{t_i : i \in \iota\})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Each $C_i$ is nonempty, so finitely many transversals exist. For a transversal
$s$, let $\rho(s)$ be the distance from the origin to $\conv(\operatorname{range}
s)$. Choose $s_0$ minimizing $\rho$, and let $p$ be the nearest point of
$\conv(\operatorname{range} s_0)$ to the origin (existing by compactness and
convexity), so $\|p\| = \rho(s_0)$. If $p = 0$, take $t = s_0$.

Otherwise $p \ne 0$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sep}, every $s_0(i)$ satisfies
$\ip{p}{x} \ge \|p\|^2$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:support} there is
$A \subseteq \operatorname{range} s_0$ with $p \in \conv(A)$ and $|A| \le d < d+1
\le |\iota|$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:pigeon} some color $j$ is free: every $a \in A$
equals $s_0(i)$ for some $i \ne j$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:near} pick $y \in C_j$ with
$\ip{p}{y} < \|p\|^2$. Replace color $j$: $s'(j) = y$, $s'(i) = s_0(i)$ otherwise.
Then $A \subseteq \operatorname{range} s'$, so $p \in \conv(\operatorname{range}
s')$, and $y \in \operatorname{range} s'$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:descent} some $q \in
\conv(\operatorname{range} s')$ has $\|q\| < \|p\|$, so $\rho(s') < \rho(s_0)$, a
contradiction. Hence $p = 0$.
\end{proof}

\section{The cone colorful Carath\'eodory theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cone Colorful Carath\'eodory]\label{thm:cone}
Let $V$ be a $d$-dimensional real inner product space and $(C_i)_{i \in \iota}$
finite color classes with $|\iota| \ge d + 1$. If each $C_i$ conically captures
the origin, then there is a colorful transversal $t$ whose range conically
captures the origin.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge} and Lemma~\ref{lem:hull}, $0 \in \conv(C_i)$ for each
$i$. Theorem~\ref{thm:main} gives a colorful transversal $t$ with
$0 \in \conv(\operatorname{range} t)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:range} yields
$\ConvexZero(\iota, t)$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge} converts it to
$\ConicZero(\iota, t)$.
\end{proof}

\section{Explicit statements in $\R^d$}

\begin{corollary}[Cone colorful Carath\'eodory in $\R^d$]
Let $C_0, \dots, C_d$ be $d+1$ finite sets of vectors in $\R^d$, each conically
capturing the origin. Then there is a colorful transversal
$t = (t_0, \dots, t_d)$ whose range conically captures the origin.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Affine colorful Carath\'eodory in $\R^d$]
Let $C_0, \dots, C_d$ be $d+1$ finite sets in $\R^d$, each with $0$ in its convex
hull. Then there is a colorful transversal $t = (t_0, \dots, t_d)$ with
$0 \in \conv(\{t_0, \dots, t_d\})$.
\end{corollary}

Both follow from Theorems~\ref{thm:cone} and~\ref{thm:main} using $\dimop \R^d = d$
and $d+1$ colors.

\section{Sharpness}

The threshold $|\iota| \ge d+1$ cannot be lowered to $d$, already for $d = 1$.
Take $C_1 = \{+1, -1\} \subseteq \R^1$: it captures the origin
($0 = \tfrac12(+1) + \tfrac12(-1)$). Any transversal selects a single
$t_1 \in \{+1, -1\}$, and $w\,t_1 = 0$ with $t_1 \ne 0$ forces $w = 0$, violating
nontriviality. So $d = 1$ color fails and $d+1 = 2$ are needed. Placing analogous
axis-aligned obstructions shows $d$ colors are insufficient in $\R^d$. This
matches the proof: the pigeonhole step needs $|A| \le d < |\iota|$, and $|A| \le d$
is the best possible hyperplane support bound.

\section{Algorithms}

The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} is a descent scheme. Maintain a transversal
$s$; compute the nearest point $p$ of $\conv(\operatorname{range} s)$ to the
origin. If $p = 0$, output $s$. Otherwise extract a Carath\'eodory support $A$ (at
most $d$ points on $\ip{p}{\cdot} = \|p\|^2$), pigeonhole a free color $j$, choose
$y \in C_j$ with $\ip{p}{y} < \|p\|^2$, set $s(j) \leftarrow y$, and repeat. Each
iteration strictly decreases $\rho(s)$. B\'ar\'any and Onn (1997) showed a related
scheme runs in polynomial time; the conical version inherits the algorithm through
the homogeneity bridge.

\section{Applications and future work}

Colorful Carath\'eodory underlies Tverberg's theorem, the first selection lemma,
centerpoints and data depth, and the feasibility of homogeneous direction systems
(the conical reading). Natural next steps: an arbitrary target point $x$; colorful
Carath\'eodory numbers and support uniqueness; colorful Helly and Tverberg;
explicit sharpness constructions in general dimension; a complexity-analyzed constructive
version; and a cone Carath\'eodory number bounding the colorful support by $d+1$.

def conic_to_convex(weights: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Rescale nonnegative conical weights (not all zero) to convex weights.

    Given w_i >= 0 with some w_j > 0, return w_i / sum(w) which are >= 0 and
    sum to 1, witnessing the convex combination of the same vanishing sum.
    """

def origin_in_convex_hull(points: Sequence[np.ndarray], tol: float = 1e-9) -> bool:
    """Return True iff 0 is a convex combination of `points`.

    Solves the feasibility LP:  find w >= 0, sum(w) = 1, sum_i w_i p_i = 0.
    """
    pts = np.asarray(points, dtype=float)
    n, d = pts.shape
    # Equality constraints: P^T w = 0  (d rows) and 1^T w = 1 (1 row).
    a_eq = np.vstack([pts.T, np.ones((1, n))])
    b_eq = np.concatenate([np.zeros(d), np.ones(1)])
    res = linprog(
        c=np.zeros(n),
        A_eq=a_eq,
        b_eq=b_eq,
        bounds=[(0.0, None)] * n,

def nearest_point_in_hull(points: Sequence[np.ndarray]) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Return (p, w): the point p of conv(points) nearest the origin, and the
    convex weights w achieving it (w >= 0, sum w = 1, p = sum_i w_i p_i)."""
    pts = np.asarray(points, dtype=float)
    n = pts.shape[0]

    def objective(w: np.ndarray) -> float:
        return float(np.dot(pts.T @ w, pts.T @ w))

    cons = ({"type": "eq", "fun": lambda w: float(np.sum(w) - 1.0)},)
    bounds = [(0.0, None)] * n

    res = minimize(objective, w0, method="SLSQP", bounds=bounds, constraints=cons)
    w = np.clip(res.x, 0.0, None)
    w = w / np.sum(w)
    return pts.T @ w, w

    "demo": """"
Numerical demonstrations of the Cone Colorful Caratheodory Theorem.

This standalone script illustrates, with concrete numerical examples:

  1. The homogeneity bridge: for the origin, a nontrivial conical combination
     can be rescaled to a convex combination, and vice versa.
  2. Testing whether the origin lies in the convex hull of a finite point set
     (equivalently, whether the set convexly captures the origin).
  3. The nearest-transversal descent algorithm that constructs a colorful
     transversal whose convex hull contains the origin, given color classes each
     of which captures the origin, with at least d+1 colors.
  4. The sharpness of the d+1 threshold: with only d colors the conclusion can
     fail (the {+1, -1} example in dimension one).

Dependencies: numpy, scipy.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import itertools
from typing import Iterable, Sequence

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linprog, minimize


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 1. The homogeneity bridge
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def conic_to_convex(weights: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """Rescale nonnegative conical weights (not all zero) to convex weights.

    Given w_i >= 0 with some w_j > 0, return w_i / sum(w) which are >= 0 and
    sum to 1, witnessing the convex combination of the same vanishing sum.
    """
    total = float(np.sum(weights))
    if total <= 0.0:
        raise ValueError("weights must be nonnegative and not all zero")
    return weights / total


def convex_to_conic(weights: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
    """A convex combination is already a conical one (identity map here)."""
    return np.array(weights, dtype=float)


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 2. Origin-in-convex-hull test
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def origin_in_convex_hull(points: Sequence[np.ndarray], tol: float = 1e-9) -> bool:
    """Return True iff 0 is a convex combination of `points`.

    Solves the feasibility LP:  find w >= 0, sum(w) = 1, sum_i w_i p_i = 0.
    """
    pts = np.asarray(points, dtype=float)
    n, d = pts.shape
    # Equality constraints: P^T w = 0  (d rows) and 1^T w = 1 (1 row).
    a_eq = np.vstack([pts.T, np.ones((1, n))])
    b_eq = np.concatenate([np.zeros(d), np.ones(1)])
    res = linprog(
        c=np.zeros(n),
        A_eq=a_eq,
        b_eq=b_eq,
        bounds=[(0.0, None)] * n,
        method="highs",
    )
    return bool(res.success) and float(np.linalg.norm(a_eq @ res.x - b_eq)) < tol


def nearest_point_in_hull(points: Sequence[np.ndarray]) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Return (p, w): the point p of conv(points) nearest the origin, and the
    convex weights w achieving it (w >= 0, sum w = 1, p = sum_i w_i p_i)."""
    pts = np.asarray(points, dtype=float)
    n = pts.shape[0]

    def objective(w: np.ndarray) -> float:
        return float(np.dot(pts.T @ w, pts.T @ w))

    cons = ({"type": "eq", "fun": lambda w: float(np.sum(w) - 1.0)},)
    bounds = [(0.0, None)] * n
    w0 = np.full(n, 1.0 / n)
    res = minimize(objective, w0, method="SLSQP", bounds=bounds, constraints=cons)
    w = np.clip(res.x, 0.0, None)
    w = w / np.sum(w)
    return pts.T @ w, w


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 3. Nearest-transversal descent for colorful Caratheodory (origin)
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def colorful_transversal_bruteforce(
    colors: Sequence[Sequence[np.ndarray]], tol: float = 1e-7
) -> list[np.ndarray] | None:
    """Find a colorful transversal (one point per color) whose convex hull
    contains the origin, by scanning all transversals.

    Guaranteed to succeed when each color captures the origin and #colors >= d+1.
    """
    for choice in itertools.product(*colors):
        p, _ = nearest_point_in_hull(list(choice))
        if float(np.linalg.norm(p)) < tol:
            return [np.asarray(c, dtype=float) for c in choice]
    return None


def colorful_transversal_descent(
    colors: Sequence[Sequence[np.ndarray]], tol: float = 1e-7, max_iter: int = 1000
) -> list[np.ndarray] | None:
    """Construct a colorful transversal capturing the origin by descent.

    Mirrors the constructive proof: start from an arbitrary transversal; while
    its nearest point p to the origin is nonzero, extract the supporting
    hyperplane <p, .> = |p|^2, find a color j whose current pick is not needed
    to represent p and which contains a near-side vertex y (<p, y> < |p|^2),
    swap it in, and repeat. Each swap strictly reduces |p|.
    """
    d = int(np.asarray(colors[0][0]).shape[0])
    if len(colors) < d + 1:
        return None
    # Initial transversal: first element of each color.
    trans: list[np.ndarray] = [np.asarray(c[0], dtype=float) for c in colors]

    for _ in range(max_iter):
        p, w = nearest_point_in_hull(trans)
        if float(np.linalg.norm(p)) < tol:
            return trans
        p_sq = float(np.dot(p, p))
        # Colors that materially support p (positive weight): "used" colors.
        used = {i for i, wi in enumerate(w) if wi > 1e-9}
        improved = False
        for j in range(len(colors)):
            if j in used:
                continue
            # Look for a near-side vertex y in color j: <p, y> < |p|^2.
            for y in colors[j]:
                y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
                if float(np.dot(p, y)) < p_sq - 1e-12:
                    trans[j] = y
                    improved = True
                    break
            if improved:
                break
        if not improved:
            # Fallback: any color/vertex strictly improving the nearest distance.
            best = float(np.linalg.norm(p))
            arg = None
            for j in range(len(colors)):
                for y in colors[j]:
                    cand = list(trans)
                    cand[j] = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
                    q, _ = nearest_point_in_hull(cand)
                    if float(np.linalg.norm(q)) < best - 1e-10:
                        best, arg = float(np.linalg.norm(q)), (j, np.asarray(y, float))
            if arg is None:
                return trans
            trans[arg[0]] = arg[1]
    return trans


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
# 4. Demonstrations
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
def demo_homogeneity_bridge() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("1. Homogeneity bridge")
    print("=" * 70)
    # Vectors summing to zero with nonnegative, non-normalized weights.
    pts = [np.array([1.0, 0.0]), np.array([-2.0, 1.0]), np.array([0.0, -1.0])]
    conic = np.array([2.0, 1.0, 1.0])  # 2*(1,0)+1*(-2,1)+1*(0,-1) = (0,0)
    combo = sum(wi * p for wi, p in zip(conic, pts))
    print(f"conical weights {conic},  weighted sum = {combo}")
    convex = conic_to_convex(conic)
    print(f"rescaled convex weights {np.round(convex, 4)},  sum = {convex.sum():.4f}")
    combo2 = sum(wi * p for wi, p in zip(convex, pts))
    print(f"convex weighted sum = {np.round(combo2, 12)}")
    print()


def demo_hull_test() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("2. Origin-in-convex-hull test")
    print("=" * 70)
    triangle = [np.array([1.0, 1.0]), np.array([-1.0, 1.0]), np.array([0.0, -1.0])]
    print(f"triangle around origin captures 0? {origin_in_convex_hull(triangle)}")
    off = [np.array([1.0, 1.0]), np.array([2.0, 1.0]), np.array([1.5, 2.0])]
    print(f"triangle avoiding origin captures 0? {origin_in_convex_hull(off)}")
    print()


def demo_colorful() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("3. Colorful Caratheodory in R^2 (need d+1 = 3 colors)")
    print("=" * 70)
    # Each color is a triangle whose hull contains the origin.
    color0 = [np.array([1.0, 0.0]), np.array([-1.0, 1.0]), np.array([-1.0, -1.0])]
    color1 = [np.array([0.0, 1.0]), np.array([1.0, -1.0]), np.array([-1.0, -1.0])]
    color2 = [np.array([-1.0, 0.0]), np.array([1.0, 1.0]), np.array([1.0, -1.0])]
    colors = [color0, color1, color2]
    for k, c in enumerate(colors):
        print(f"  color {k} captures origin? {origin_in_convex_hull(c)}")
    trans = colorful_transversal_descent(colors)
    assert trans is not None
    print("  descent transversal:", [tuple(np.round(v, 3)) for v in trans])
    print(f"  transversal captures origin? {origin_in_convex_hull(trans)}")
    bf = colorful_transversal_bruteforce(colors)
    print(f"  brute-force also finds one? {bf is not None}")
    print()


def demo_sharpness() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("4. Sharpness: d colors can fail (d = 1)")
    print("=" * 70)
    color = [np.array([1.0]), np.array([-1.0])]  # single color captures 0
    print(f"  single color {{+1,-1}} captures 0? {origin_in_convex_hull(color)}")
    # With only ONE color (d = 1, need d+1 = 2), every transversal is a single
    # nonzero number -> cannot capture the origin.
    any_ok = any(
        origin_in_convex_hull([np.asarray(t[0], float)])
        for t in itertools.product(color)
    )
    print(f"  any single-color transversal captures 0? {any_ok}  (expected False)")
    # With TWO copies of the color (2 colors, d+1 = 2), a transversal succeeds.
    colors2 = [color, color]
    trans = colorful_transversal_bruteforce(colors2)
    print(f"  with 2 colors, transversal found? {trans is not None}")
    if trans is not None:
        print(f"    transversal = {[float(v[0]) for v in trans]}")
    print()


def main() -> None:
    np.set_printoptions(suppress=True)
    demo_homogeneity_bridge()
    demo_hull_test()
    demo_colorful()
    demo_sharpness()
    print("All demonstrations completed.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Future Directions — Log-Concavity in the d-Hoggatt Hierarchy

This cycle formalized (in `HoggattTotals.lean`) the **sharp `d = 1` vs `d = 2`
dichotomy** for the *total* d-Hoggatt numbers `H_d(n) = ∑_k H_d(n,k)`, together
with the general mechanism and its tropical reformulation:

* **`d = 1`** (`H_1(n) = 2^n`): **log-linear**, `H(n+1)² = H(n)·H(n+2)`, hence
  log-concave and log-convex with equality and *not* strictly log-convex
  (`pow_two_logLinear`, `pow_two_not_strictLogConvex`).
* **`d = 2`** (`H_2(n) = Cₙ`, Catalan): **strictly log-convex**,
  `H(n+1)² < H(n)·H(n+2)`, and *not* log-concave
  (`catalan_strictLogConvex`, `catalan_not_logConcave`).
* Combined statement: `sharp_dichotomy`.
* Engine: the exact **discriminant identity**
  `(2n+1)(n+3)·Cₙ·Cₙ₊₂ = (n+2)(2n+3)·Cₙ₊₁²` (`catalan_discriminant`), whose
  coefficients differ by the positive constant `3`.
* General criterion (Conjecture 2 mechanism): a positive real sequence with
  strictly increasing consecutive ratios is strictly log-convex
  (`strictLogConvex_real_of_ratio_strictMono`), with the Catalan totals exhibited
  as a concrete instance via strictly increasing ratios `Cₙ₊₁/Cₙ < Cₙ₊₂/Cₙ₊₁`
  (`catalan_ratio_strictMono`).
* Tropical dequantization (Conjecture 5): strict log-convexity is exactly strict
  convexity of `log H` / strict concavity of the valuation `v = −log H`
  (`strictLogConvex_iff_log`).

All results compile against Mathlib `v4.28.0` with only the standard axioms
(`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`) and contain no `sorry`.

## Next targets

### Conjecture 1 — Universal log-convexity of the totals for `d ≥ 2`
Empirically verified here for Baxter (`d = 3`) on the first several terms. A
uniform proof would ideally come from a `d`-independent two-term recurrence
producing a discriminant identity with a positive coefficient gap, generalizing
`catalan_discriminant`. The Baxter recurrence
`(n+3)(n+2)B(n+1) = (n+1)(8n²+ ... )` is a natural next case to formalize.

### Conjecture 2 — Row-sum log-convexity as a summation phenomenon
The `ℝ`-level criterion `strictLogConvex_real_of_ratio_strictMono` isolates the
ratio-amplification mechanism. The remaining step is a triangle-level statement:
log-concave rows with a nondecreasing row-ratio `T(n+1,k)/T(n,k)` give log-convex
row sums (a Chebyshev-sum / rearrangement inequality). This is a clean,
Mathlib-tractable target via `Finset.inner_mul_le_norm_mul_norm`-style
rearrangement lemmas.

### Conjecture 3 — Infinite log-concavity of the rows
Requires formalizing the log-concavity operator `𝓛` and the golden-ratio-squared
closure constant `(3+√5)/2`. The dichotomy tools here (log-linearity of `2^n`,
the ℝ-criterion) are prerequisites for the closure lemma.

### Conjecture 4 — Log-concave renormalization of the totals
For `d = 2`, the exact Catalan growth ratio `(n+2)(2n+3)/((2n+1)(n+3))` (readable
straight off `catalan_discriminant`) is the concrete `w_2` candidate to divide
out; the residual sequence is the object to test for infinite log-concavity.

### Conjecture 5 — Tropical dequantization
`strictLogConvex_iff_log` supplies the base equivalence. The iterated version —
infinite log-concavity ⇔ iterated finite differences of `v` keep a fixed sign —
is the piecewise-linear/tropical statement to build next.
